paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1930s, the linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf claimed that speakers of different languages perceive the world differently because their languages carve up reality in different ways. His most famous example, that the Hopi language lacks words for time and therefore its speakers lack the concept, has been thoroughly discredited. Yet the underlying question, whether language influences thought, has returned to scientific respectability, and the evidence now suggests a more subtle picture than either Whorf or his critics imagined.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider colour. Russian has separate basic terms for light blue and dark blue, whereas English uses a single term, blue, for both. In experiments, Russian speakers were faster at distinguishing shades that straddle their linguistic boundary than shades that fall on the same side of it, while English speakers showed no such advantage. Strikingly, the effect disappeared when participants were given a verbal task, such as repeating digits, to occupy their language processing, which suggests that language was actively contributing to the judgement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Space provides another example. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of Australia, do not use left and right but absolute directions: one might say there is an ant on your south-east leg. Such speakers maintain an extraordinary sense of orientation, even in unfamiliar places. Researchers argue that the habit of tracking direction, enforced by grammar from early childhood, trains this ability. English speakers can be taught to do likewise, but it takes deliberate effort.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These findings do not support the strong claim that language determines what can be thought. Speakers of languages without a particular word can still understand the concept, as shown by the ease with which words are borrowed. The effects are better described as differences in habit and speed: language makes some distinctions more habitual, and therefore cheaper to process. Critics note that many demonstrations involve small differences in reaction time, whose significance for everyday life is uncertain, and that some results have proved difficult to replicate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most defensible conclusion is therefore a modest one. Language is a tool for thought, and as with any tool, its shape guides how we use it without limiting what we can do. That may disappoint those who hope for a dramatic revelation about alien minds, but it has the merit of fitting the evidence. It also reminds us that translation is neither impossible nor trivial: we can convey what another language expresses, but we must sometimes work harder to do so.
